Chapter Eight: The Persistence of Stereotypes in the Modern Era
Even as America changes, some things just don’t seem to budge. Those old stereotypes—like "white trash" and "redneck"—they haven’t disappeared. They’ve just put on new clothes, showing up in different forms, but still doing the same old job: telling us who counts, and who supposedly doesn’t.
Picture this. A young woman is scrolling through her feed, and she spots yet another joke about "trailer trash" or a meme poking fun at rural accents. She might laugh along, not wanting to look uptight or sensitive, but deep down, the message lands. People like her? Still seen as less than—objects of ridicule, or maybe just pity.
The shame isn’t loud anymore, but it lingers. It quietly shapes how she thinks about herself, and where she fits in.
But here’s something to pay attention to: these stereotypes don’t just stick around by accident. They actually serve a purpose. By making poverty into a joke, or treating it like a personal flaw, society gets to skip the tough questions—like why some folks keep getting left behind. Most people don’t even notice how these stories start to settle in, shaping what they believe, and making it easier to turn away from someone else’s struggle.
If you watch politics, you’ll notice something. People almost never talk about class out in the open. Instead, the conversation shifts to words like "values," "culture," or "personal responsibility." The old idea that being poor means you’ve failed? It’s still incredibly strong, even though there’s so much evidence that tells a different story. The myth that America is a classless society lives on—because it’s easier to pretend those facing hardship are just rare exceptions, not the result of a system that lifts some up while pushing others down.
And it’s not just politics. Popular culture keeps these ideas alive, too. Movies, TV shows, news stories—they tend to zoom in on the most outrageous or dramatic examples, turning real lives into entertainment. The people at the heart of these stories almost never get to share their side. Their challenges get trimmed down to punchlines, or warnings of what not to become.
But you know what? There are signs that things are shifting. More writers, artists, and activists from working-class backgrounds are stepping up, telling their own stories, and pushing back against those tired old labels. Their voices sometimes get drowned out by the endless noise of the culture wars, but they’re still there—insisting that their experiences matter, and that they deserve to be seen for who they really are.
So, what’s the real takeaway here? The fact that these stereotypes are still hanging around is proof that class divisions haven’t gone anywhere. They’re still shaping lives and choices in ways that often go unnoticed. The shame and stigma attached to being poor and white are still powerful—but they don’t have to be permanent.
